abstract: We present RESPLE2, a recursive multi-sensor state estimation framework using non-uniform B-splines for 6-DoF motion representation. By exploiting the knot-clamping boundary property, we propose a theoretically grounded mechanism for exact control-point prediction directly informed by inertial kinematics along the trajectory, with knot placement adapted to motion and measurement availability. Within an iterated extended Kalman filter, we perform this prediction using a subset of inertial measurements. A subsequent reset step preserves trajectory consistency as the knots extend. The update step further incorporates heterogeneous sensor measurements at their native timestamps through continuous-time observation models, supporting flexible combinations of LiDARs, cameras, inertial measurement units, and leg kinematics. We further develop a lightweight global optimization module that directly refines non-uniform B-spline control points by incorporating loop-closure constraints derived from LiDAR-visual cues. We conduct extensive evaluations on public and experimental datasets across handheld, tracked, legged, and hybrid aerial-legged platforms, covering highly dynamic maneuvers with extreme accelerations. Compared with state-of-the-art multi-sensor odometry systems, RESPLE2 achieves competitive or superior estimation accuracy and robustness in the corresponding sensor configurations, particularly under aggressive motion, while maintaining real-time operation. We publicly release our code and experimental datasets at https://github.com/ASIG-X/RESPLE2.

sections.body: Accurate 6-DoF egomotion matters for legged, tracked, and hybrid robots. Most existing odometry systems are sensor-specific and were validated mainly on aerial and wheeled platforms. Conventional filters and sliding-window optimizers approximate asynchronous sensors and scale poorly as sensor rates change. Uniform-knot B-spline recursive estimation (RESPLE) uses one globally fixed knot interval, which limits accuracy during aggressive motion. Existing B-spline systems lack exact kinematic prediction of new control points and native loop closure. The paper proposes RESPLE2, a recursive non-uniform B-spline estimator in an iterated extended Kalman filter. Its contributions are exact control-point prediction from inertial measurements, a global refinement module for loop closure, a unified LO, LIO, LVIO, LKIO, and LKVIO design, and evaluation on legged, tracked, and hybrid platforms.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing multi-sensor odometry is sensor-specific, and uniform B-spline estimators cannot predict control points from inertial data.

sections.body: Discrete-time systems such as FAST-LIVO2 and Point-LIO fuse LiDAR, camera, and inertial data with filtering. Leg-KILO adds leg joint measurements for quadrupedal odometry. CTE-MLO pairs a Gaussian process representation with an extended Kalman filter for LiDAR-only odometry. B-spline systems such as CLINS, SLICT2, and Coco-LIC use sliding-window optimization. For new control points, RESPLE uses a constant transition matrix, SLICT2 adds an integrated IMU offset to the endpoint, and Coco-LIC copies the most recent control points. The authors state that none of these predicts control points exactly from kinematics. For loop closure, CLINS applies a two-stage correction, while RESPLE2 detects loops with iBTC and refines control points directly.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior B-spline systems either predict control points without exact kinematics or lack native loop-closure refinement.

sections.body: The trajectory is a cubic B-spline over non-uniform knots, with position and orientation as separate components. Each query time uses four local control points and six local knots, with a basis matrix from the non-uniform spline formulation. Orientation uses a cumulative basis built from tangent-space increments between adjacent control points. Velocity, acceleration, and angular velocity follow from the same basis. The state of the TriS model is the set of recurrent control points, estimated recursively with an extended Kalman filter. The section notes that the standard transition matrix propagates control points from earlier knot intervals without current kinematic information. This can yield inaccurate priors during rapid changes in motion and weak data association in degenerate scenes.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Cubic non-uniform B-splines and their kinematics define the recursive state of the four most recent control points.

sections.body: Incoming LiDAR scans are downsampled with voxel-grid filtering. Inertial samples are split by alternating assignment into a prediction subset and an update subset. Camera images are undistorted, and features are tracked with a KLT sparse optical-flow tracker. Leg joint measurements are converted to foot positions and velocities with forward kinematics. When the criteria for a new knot are met, the knot is clamped to the spline endpoint, and its control point is predicted from the prediction subset. The previous endpoint knot is unclamped, and a reset corrects the control points and covariance over the finalized spacing. Buffered measurements are then fused in the iterated update. After convergence, the voxel map is updated, and new image features receive depth from LiDAR points. Estimated control points then go to global refinement, where iBTC detects loop closures.
sections.heading: System Overview
sections.headline: RESPLE2 predicts each new control point from inertial samples, resets the spline, then runs an iterated update.

sections.body: The augmented state has 30 dimensions: four six-dimensional control points, each holding a position and an orientation increment, plus accelerometer and gyroscope biases. The process model clamps each new knot at the spline boundary with multiplicity three. At that boundary the trajectory passes through the newest control point. The velocity there is proportional to the difference between the last two position control points, divided by the last knot interval. Angular velocity is likewise set by the last orientation increment. Because of this property, the newest control point can be predicted by integrating IMU measurements along the trajectory. Derivations are given in an appendix. The measurement models cover LiDAR, camera, inertial, and leg kinematics at their native timestamps.
sections.heading: Generalized Spline State-Space Modeling with Multi-Sensor Measurements
sections.headline: Clamping each new knot lets the control point be predicted exactly from inertial measurements.

sections.body: The augmented state is initialized from the previous posterior. The new knot's position and orientation control points start at the previous endpoint values, with a zero orientation increment. The filter then propagates the augmented mean and covariance over the prediction IMU substeps, using the process model and its Jacobians. The update repeatedly relinearizes the measurement models until the state increment falls below a threshold or a maximum iteration count is reached. It then gives the posterior state and covariance. The legged-kinematic Jacobians for the zero-velocity part are derived explicitly, while the LiDAR, IMU, and camera Jacobians follow prior work. This section does not report a numerical evaluation of these steps.
sections.heading: Inertial-Informed Iterated Extended Kalman Filter on Non-Uniform B-Splines
sections.headline: The iterated extended Kalman filter propagates an augmented 33-dimensional state over inertial substeps, then updates.

sections.body: Loop closures are detected with iBTC between the current LiDAR scan and historical keyframes in the LiDAR-visual-inertial setting. Keyframes are aggregated into submaps, and candidates are verified by geometric registration. Accepted matches give relative six-DoF transforms as constraints. The global optimization minimizes two residual sets. Loop-closure residuals constrain the relative translation and rotation between poses at paired timestamps. Odometry residuals constrain the relative translation and rotation between consecutive control points. Each odometry residual involves only two control points, which keeps the system sparse. Loop-closure residuals require spline interpolation. The problem is solved with the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. The section states that higher-order kinematics such as angular and linear velocity are preserved; quantitative results appear in the evaluation section.
sections.heading: Global Refinement
sections.headline: Loop-closure constraints refine all control points by least squares while odometry residuals keep adjacent control points consistent.

sections.body: RESPLE2 is a ROS2 package with separate odometry and global refinement nodes, each typically using five OpenMP threads. Variants are LIO, LVIO, LKIO, LKVIO, and a LiDAR-only variant that replaces the inertial process model with a constant-velocity model. Baselines are Coco-LIC, FAST-LIVO2, CTE-MLO, Point-LIO, Leg-KILO, and RESPLE with VoxelMap. Errors are computed with the evo package. On the handheld sequences, RESPLE2 completes all evaluated sequences for LIO and LVIO. On az-corri, the RESPLE2 LIO variant reaches 6.166 meters RMSE, compared with 44.057 for RESPLE and 46.476 for FAST-LIVO2.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: On every handheld sequence, RESPLE2 has at least one variant with the lowest odometry error.

sections.body: In an ablation on the enclosed legged-quadcopter sequences, inertial-informed prediction reduces position APE on every sequence, with relative reductions of approximately 39%-76%. The largest reduction is on high1, which has extremely high accelerations. The baseline uses a constant transition matrix with identical knot intervals, which isolates the effect of prediction. For knot placement, RESPLE2 uses 2087 control points on flip1, compared with 2362 for Coco-LIC, a reduction of 11.6%, while achieving higher accuracy. Per-frame runtime uses 15.4%, 18.3%, and 10.6% of the available time budget on flip1 (LIO), `day_open` (LVIO), and Outdoor1 (LKIO). RCP prediction and reset take at most 0.51 ms per frame. The latest global optimization takes about 2 s.
sections.heading: Further Discussions
sections.headline: Inertial-informed prediction lowers position error on all legged-quadcopter sequences, and knots concentrate near ground impacts.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes RESPLE2 as a recursive non-uniform B-spline estimator. Its knot-clamping property gives direct IMU-based control-point prediction, and a reset preserves local trajectory consistency. A global module refines control points using loop-closure constraints. The framework supports LiDAR, visual, inertial, and leg-kinematic combinations, as well as LiDAR-only operation. The authors report accuracy comparable to or exceeding that of the compared baselines, particularly under aggressive motion and severe IMU saturation, while maintaining real-time operation. Stated future work includes adaptive sensor weighting, visual feature constraints that do not depend on LiDAR-derived depth, and integration with onboard motion planning.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Reported accuracy matches or exceeds baselines in real time, with visual constraints independent of LiDAR depth left as future work.
